subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a:
questions.explain: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton (H⁺); a base accepts one.

questions.q: For a titration of a weak base with a strong acid, the equivalence point pH is below 7, so the best indicator is:
questions.explain: The equivalence point lies in the acidic region, matching methyl orange's range (3.1–4.4).

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the units of Kc are:
questions.explain: Kc = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] gives (mol dm⁻³)²/(mol dm⁻³) = mol dm⁻³.

questions.q: Which change alters the value of the equilibrium constant Kc for a given reaction?
options: Changing the concentration of a reactant
questions.explain: Only a change in temperature changes the value of Kc; concentration, pressure and catalysts do not.

questions.q: In an ethanoic acid/ethanoate buffer, when a small amount of acid (H⁺) is added it is removed by reaction with:
questions.explain: Added H⁺ reacts with the conjugate base CH₃COO⁻ to form CH₃COOH, limiting the pH change.

questions.q: Removing product continuously from an equilibrium system causes the equilibrium to:
options: shift to the right to replace the product
questions.explain: By Le Chatelier, removing product drives the reaction forward to partially replace what was removed.

questions.q: Which combination produces a titration curve with NO sharp vertical pH jump at the equivalence point, making indicators unsuitable?
questions.explain: A weak acid–weak base titration has only a gradual pH change, so no indicator gives a sharp endpoint.

questions.q: A buffer contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ weak acid (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵) and 0.20 mol dm⁻³ of its salt. The pH is:
questions.explain: With [acid] = [salt], [H⁺] = Ka = 10⁻⁵, so pH = pKa = 5.0.

questions.q: For a titration of a strong acid with a strong base, which indicator is suitable?
questions.explain: A strong acid–strong base titration has a large vertical pH range spanning both indicators' ranges, so either works.

questions.q: What is the pH of a solution with [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³?
For a weak acid HA, the acid dissociation constant Ka is given by:
questions.explain: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] for the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻.

questions.q: At 25 °C, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. The pH of pure water is:
questions.explain: In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = √Kw = 10⁻⁷, so pH = 7.0 (neutral at 25 °C).

questions.q: In the equilibrium HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, which species is the conjugate base of HCl?
questions.explain: Removing a proton from HCl gives its conjugate base, Cl⁻.

questions.q: The mole fraction of a gas is 0.25 and the total pressure is 200 kPa. Its partial pressure is:
questions.explain: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = 0.25 × 200 = 50 kPa.

questions.q: A buffer has [acid] = 0.10 and [salt] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Using [H⁺] = Ka × [acid]/[salt], pH is approximately:
A strong monobasic acid differs from a weak monobasic acid because the strong acid:
options: has a larger Ka but does not fully dissociate
questions.explain: A strong acid is, by definition, fully (essentially completely) dissociated in aqueous solution.

questions.q: An acidic buffer is typically made from:
options: a weak base and a strong acid
a strong acid and its salt
a weak acid and its salt (conjugate base)
questions.explain: An acidic buffer contains a weak acid plus its conjugate base (e.g. CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻).

questions.q: The pH of a 0.010 mol dm⁻³ solution of a strong monobasic acid (e.g. HCl) is:
questions.explain: For a fully dissociated strong acid [H⁺] = 0.010, so pH = −log(10⁻²) = 2.0.

questions.q: A catalyst is added to a system at equilibrium. What happens to the position of equilibrium?
options: It shifts towards the exothermic direction
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not shift the equilibrium position.

questions.q: What are the units of Kc for the reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)?
questions.explain: With equal moles of gas on both sides the concentration terms cancel, so Kc is dimensionless.

questions.q: For an exothermic forward reaction, increasing the temperature will:
options: leave Kc unchanged but shift left
decrease Kc and shift equilibrium left
increase Kc and shift equilibrium right
questions.explain: Raising temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, decreasing Kc and shifting equilibrium towards reactants.

questions.q: Which expression correctly represents Kp for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)?
questions.explain: Kp uses partial pressures of products over reactants each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

questions.q: For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, what is the effect of increasing the total pressure?
options: No change because moles are equal on both sides
The position of equilibrium shifts to the left
The position of equilibrium shifts to the right
questions.explain: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (2 vs 4), i.e. towards NH₃ on the right.

questions.q: A weak acid has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Its pKa is:
questions.explain: pKa = −log Ka = −log(10⁻⁵) = 5.0.

questions.q: For a reaction at equilibrium, if Kc is very large (e.g. 10⁶), this indicates:
options: The equilibrium mixture is mostly products
The equilibrium mixture is mostly reactants
questions.explain: A large Kc means the numerator (products) dominates, so the position of equilibrium lies far to the right.

questions.q: Calculate the pH of a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solution of a weak acid with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ (assume [H⁺] = √(Ka × c)).
At the half-neutralisation (half-equivalence) point in a weak acid–strong base titration:
questions.explain: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻], so [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 25 °C? (log 5 ≈ 0.70)
For a titration of a weak acid with a strong base, the most suitable indicator is:
questions.explain: The equivalence pH is above 7, in phenolphthalein's range (8.3–10), so phenolphthalein is appropriate.

questions.q: For the reaction 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), increasing pressure at constant temperature shifts the equilibrium:
questions.explain: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (1 mol N₂O₄ vs 2 mol NO₂), shifting right.
